title: SIP – What Next?
blurb: What comes after a SIP starts: step-up, pause, renewal, the glide path, withdrawals and the behaviour that breaks the habit.

rows: New employees (all sections), sales team (talk-tracks, role-plays) and investors as awareness material
One 60–75 minute session, plus 20 minutes of role-play and the quiz
Module 9 (goal-based investing), Module 10 (XIRR vs CAGR) and Module 11 (the wrong time to invest); NISM Series V-A and an EUIN before dealing with clients
Each L.E.A.R.N. stage has: what to know, how to do it, a talk-track, and the investor takeaway
outcomes: Name the seven decision points in a SIP's life, from step-up to goal reached.
Ask the right questions before advising a client to step up, pause, stop, extend or redeem.
Explain what to do when a SIP's end date arrives or a goal is 1–3 years away.
Use STP and SWP correctly when moving money out of equity.
Run an annual SIP review and handle the behaviour that derails SIPs.
Stay within compliance: no return promises, no tax advice, every decision recorded.

sources: SEBI letter of 3 January 2024 on SIP auto-cancellation after consecutive failed instalments (in force April 2024)
Cafemutual (Dec 2024): SIP cancellation to be processed within 2 working days from 1 December 2024
AMFI guidance on SIP pause and top-up facilities; AMC scheme forms for pause and step-up terms
Income-tax Act and Finance Act provisions on capital gains from mutual funds (verify current rates each year)

lessons.title: A SIP is a habit, not a product
The end date is not the goal date
Each instalment is its own purchase
Four checks before any SIP change
Six client sentences, and what to ask
Time to goal decides the next step
When the goal is years away: renew
The glide path: step down, not jump off
SWP: how long does the money last?
Three checks before money moves out
What derails SIPs, and what to say

a: A SIP is a habit, not a product. Our job is to protect the habit through every decision that follows.
Step-up, pause, missed debit, market fall, end date, goal near, goal reached.
₹10,000 a month for 15 years at 12%: flat ≈ ₹50.5 L; with a 10% yearly step-up ≈ ₹86.8 L.
Every year or after a raise, but only after the emergency fund and loans are covered.
When a SIP's tenure ends, only instalments stop. Units stay invested until redeemed.
₹10,000 for 10 years ≈ ₹23.2 L. Held 10 more years ≈ ₹72.2 L; renewed ≈ ₹99.9 L.
Since April 2024: a monthly SIP is cancelled after 3 consecutive failed debits; quarterly or less often after 2.
Since 1 December 2024, SIP cancellation requests are processed within 2 working days (earlier 10).
A pause skips instalments for a few months and then resumes; a stop ends the SIP. Pause terms vary by AMC.
A 6-month pause in a 15-year SIP: ≈ ₹48.3 L vs ≈ ₹50.5 L. A short pause costs little.
Goal, time left, cash flow, progress (by XIRR). Ask why before acting.
7+ yrs: renew and step up. 3–7: plan glide. 1–3: STP to debt. Under 1: mostly liquid. Reached: staged redemption or SWP.
Equity about 65% at 3 years out, 45% at 2, 25% at 1, close to 0% at the goal for money to be spent.
Keep 1–2 years of withdrawals in a liquid or short-duration fund so falls don't force equity sales.
Check exit load (per instalment, FIFO), tax (refer to a CA), and nominee, bank and KYC details.
A SIP that rises by a set amount or % each year.
Example: ₹10,000 rising 10% a year.
Remember: the biggest lever after starting early.
Temporarily skipping instalments without cancelling.
Example: 3-month pause after a job change.
Remember: better than stopping or redeeming.
The date registered instalments stop.
Example: 10-year SIP ends in 2026; goal is 2034.
Remember: units stay invested; renew if the goal is far.
SIP cancelled after consecutive failed debits.
Example: monthly SIP fails 3 times in a row.
Remember: fix the mandate after the first failure.
Cancellation processed within 2 working days.
Example: request on Monday, done by Wednesday.
Remember: in force since 1 Dec 2024.
Oldest units are treated as redeemed first.
Example: year-1 units redeemed before year-5 units.
Remember: each instalment has its own date.
A charge on redemptions within a set period.
Example: often 1% within 1 year (varies by scheme).
Remember: recent instalments may still carry it.
Planned shift from equity to debt as a goal nears.
Example: equity 65% → 45% → 25% → ~0%.
Remember: step down, don't jump off.
Regular transfers from one scheme to another.
Example: monthly transfer from equity to a liquid fund.
Remember: spreads the exit; each transfer is a redemption.
Systematic Withdrawal Plan: fixed regular redemptions.
Example: ₹45,000 a month from ₹50 L.
Remember: the withdrawal rate decides how long it lasts.
Redeeming as payments fall due.
Example: college fees paid each term from a debt fund.
Remember: keep the rest invested meanwhile.
A yearly check of goal, progress, mix and admin.
Example: 20-minute review each April.
Remember: plus extra reviews after life events.
Redeeming because the value looks big.
Example: "It's doubled, let's enjoy it."
Remember: ask whether it is the goal money.
Spending rises with income; the SIP does not.
Example: raise received, SIP unchanged.
Remember: step up while the raise is fresh.
Many overlapping SIPs.
Example: 12 SIPs holding the same stocks.
Remember: fewer, well-chosen funds.
A retiree draws from a liquid fund during a fall so equity is never sold at the bottom.
Example: one year of withdrawals kept aside.
Remember: the buffer protects the plan, not just the money.

questions.q: What happens to existing units when a SIP's end date arrives?
o: They move into a liquid fund
They are frozen in the folio
questions.why: Only the instalments stop. The units stay invested until the investor redeems them.

questions.q: How many consecutive failed debits cancel a monthly SIP?
questions.why: Three for monthly or more frequent SIPs; two for quarterly or less frequent SIPs.

questions.q: Within how many working days must a SIP cancellation be processed?
questions.why: Two working days since 1 December 2024, down from ten.

questions.q: In the illustration, a 10% yearly step-up on ₹10,000 for 15 years grows to about…
questions.why: About ₹86.8 L at an assumed 12%, against ₹50.5 L flat, with about ₹38.1 L invested instead of ₹18.0 L.

questions.q: What does pausing a SIP do?
o: Skips instalments for a while and then resumes
questions.why: A pause skips instalments for a few months and then resumes; a stop ends the SIP. A pause keeps the habit and the units intact.

questions.q: On a redemption, which units are treated as sold first?
questions.why: FIFO means first in, first out: the oldest units are redeemed first, so each instalment's own purchase date decides its exit load and tax.

questions.q: Which four checks come before any SIP change?
o: The fund's last month return, the market level, the AMC and the tax rate
Goal, time left, cash flow and progress
Number of SIPs, folio count, bank and nominee
Past returns, star rating, AUM and expense ratio
questions.why: Goal, time left, cash flow and progress. The request itself is never the reason.

questions.q: A client says, "I want to stop my SIP." What is the first move?
o: Ask whether it is cash flow, a market fall, a goal change or fund doubts
questions.why: The cause decides the fix: pause for cash flow, stay for a fall, re-plan for a goal change, review the fund for doubts.

questions.q: A client gets a raise and wants a bigger SIP. What comes first?
o: Step up by the whole raise immediately
Check the emergency fund and any costly loans
Stop the old SIP and start fresh
Invest the raise as a lump sum in a sectoral fund
questions.why: Step up only after basics are covered. A step-up the client cannot sustain is the first thing cancelled.

questions.q: A client's SIP has ended but the goal is 8 years away. What is the best next step?
o: Renew the SIP, ideally with a step-up
questions.why: With years to go, renewing adds contributions and keeps the habit. Calendar the new end date.

questions.q: A client's goal is 8 years away and the SIP has just ended. What is the next step?
o: Renew or extend the SIP, and step up each year
questions.why: With 7+ years to go, renew and step up. Staged redemption and SWP come much later.

questions.q: Which is the illustrative glide path for a goal three, two and one year away?
questions.why: Equity steps down as the goal approaches: about 65%, 45%, 25%, and close to 0% at the goal for money to be spent.

questions.q: What is a glide path?
o: A gradual, stepped shift from equity to debt as the goal nears
Moving all the money on one day
Selling everything when the goal arrives
Switching funds every year for higher returns
questions.why: It is a stepped shift over one to three years, not one big switch.

questions.q: ₹10,000 a month for 10 years, then 10 more years: what does the illustration show?
o: About ₹72.2 L if held; about ₹99.9 L if renewed
About ₹99.9 L if held; about ₹72.2 L if renewed
questions.why: Holding reaches about ₹72.2 L; renewing reaches about ₹99.9 L, because renewal adds ten more years of contributions.

questions.q: What does an SWP do?
o: Redeems a fixed amount at regular intervals
questions.why: A Systematic Withdrawal Plan redeems a fixed amount at regular intervals, which is how a retiree takes income.

questions.q: ₹50 lakh at an assumed 8%: roughly how long does ₹45,000 a month last?
questions.why: About 17 years in the illustration. It is not a promise.

questions.q: Why keep 1–2 years of withdrawals in a liquid fund?
o: So a market fall does not force equity sales at low prices
questions.why: The buffer pays the client through a fall so the equity portion is not sold at the bottom.

questions.q: Which three checks come before a redemption, switch, STP or SWP?
o: Exit load, tax, and nominee/bank/KYC details
The fund manager's tenure, the AUM and the star rating
The AMC's office address and the folio number
questions.why: Exit load per instalment, the tax position (referred to a CA), and current nominee, bank and KYC details.

questions.q: Which of these is a redemption that may be taxed?
o: Every STP transfer and SWP withdrawal
questions.why: Every switch, STP transfer and SWP withdrawal is a redemption, so gains on it may be taxed. Refer the client to a CA.

questions.q: How should progress towards a goal be measured in the annual review?
questions.why: XIRR handles SIP cash flows correctly; absolute return hides the effect of timing.

questions.q: When should a SIP be reviewed?
o: Once a year, plus after any major life event
questions.why: Every SIP gets an annual review, and an extra one after a job change, marriage, a child, a loan, a bonus or retirement.

questions.q: A SIP ends in nine months. What should the review do?
o: Ignore it; the AMC will call
Note it and plan the renewal now
questions.why: Note SIPs ending in the next 12 months and plan renewals; the call goes three months before the end date.

questions.q: A stable-income client wants to stop a SIP after a 15% fall, with the goal 12 years away. Best response?
o: Stop the SIP until markets settle
Pause only if cash is tight; a fall is when the SIP buys the most units
Redeem and wait for a better entry
questions.why: With a stable income and a long goal, the habit should continue. A pause is for a cash crunch, not for a fall.

questions.q: A client says, "It's doubled! Let's take it out." What is the first question?
o: Which fund should we buy next?
Is this the money for your goal?
How much tax will you pay?
questions.why: Link the decision to the goal. If it is goal money, stay the course; a separate fun fund can cover the celebration.

questions.q: A client wants to switch because a friend's fund did better last year. What do you do?
o: Switch immediately to capture the gains
Compare 3–5 year records against the benchmark first
questions.why: One year is noise. Compare three to five year records against the benchmark and category before any switch.

questions.q: A client has 12 SIPs holding overlapping funds. What is the right advice?
o: Many hold the same stocks; fewer, well-chosen funds are easier to track
Cancel them all and start over
Move them all to one sectoral fund
questions.why: Overlapping funds add complexity, not diversification. Consolidate where it is sensible.

questions.q: Which statement is compliant?
o: "Illustratively, at 8% assumed, ₹40,000 a month could last about 22 years; not guaranteed."
questions.why: Label projections illustrative, state the assumption, and make no promise.

questions.q: A client asks how much tax the redemption will attract. What do you do?
o: Work it out and tell them the exact amount
Explain that redemptions may be taxed and refer them to a CA
questions.why: We explain that a redemption may be taxed and refer the calculation to the client's CA. We do not give tax advice.

questions.q: Anil's 10-year SIP has ended and his goal is 8 years away. What is the best next step?
o: Redeem everything and move to a fixed deposit
Renew the SIP, ideally with a step-up, and calendar the end date
Stop the SIP; the goal is only 8 years away
Switch to a small-cap fund for higher returns
questions.why: With 8 years to the goal, renewing adds contributions while the existing units keep compounding. Calendar the new end date.

questions.q: Sana's monthly SIP has failed twice in a row. What must happen now?
o: Fix or re-register the mandate now, because a third consecutive failure cancels the SIP
Cancel the SIP and start a new one
Change her bank account without telling her
questions.why: Three consecutive failures cancel a monthly SIP, so the mandate is fixed after the first, definitely after the second.
